title: Consumers are beginning to use AI as a telecoms-market intermediary while retaining demand for human support and accountable access
source_unit: Ofcom, Consumers using AI to help manage their telecoms services, but human contact still valued, 25 September 2026
geography: Online adults and small businesses in the United Kingdom using phone, broadband, and pay-TV markets

observations.period: 2026; AI use in consumer telecoms journeys

denominator.unit: Ofcom Technology Tracker online-adult user frame

general_ai_use.unit: percent of adult UK internet users who interacted with a GenAI tool and/or AI customer-service chatbot in the prior 12 months

telecom_ai_use.unit: percent of online adults using an AI tool in relation to telecoms services

issue_resolution.unit: percent using AI to resolve a telecoms issue

comparison_complaint.value: 3% use AI for price, product, or service comparison and 2% use it to make a complaint

agency_route.value: AI is moving from general experimentation into concrete consumer navigation, comparison, and remedy-seeking

observations.method: Ofcom review drawing on Technology Tracker research and qualitative research on consumer experiences and attitudes.
observations.uncertainty: The publication does not establish whether AI use improves prices, resolution time, service quality, complaint outcomes, or consumer welfare.
observations.subgroup: Online adults, small businesses, telecoms customers, people resolving issues, people comparing services, and people making complaints.
observations.counterinterpretation: Early use may reflect novelty or limited availability rather than a durable shift in how consumers manage essential services.

mixed_preference.value: some participants prefer AI to human interaction, while others value human empathy, compassion, and the ability to understand complex problems

human_route.value: speaking to a person remains particularly valued for complex or sensitive issues

trust_problem.value: some participants doubt whether AI can understand the issue or produce a useful resolution

service_route.value: automation does not eliminate the need for human escalation; it changes the boundary between convenience and accountable support

observations.method: Ofcom qualitative research reported alongside Technology Tracker findings.
observations.uncertainty: Qualitative participants illustrate a range of views and are not representative of all UK telecoms customers.
observations.subgroup: Consumers preferring convenience, consumers with complex or sensitive issues, people with low AI trust, and small businesses.
observations.counterinterpretation: Improved agent design, context retention, and clear escalation could increase trust without requiring human contact for every routine task.

observations.period: 2026 onward; personal AI agents in telecoms markets

agentic_use.value: future AI agents could select better broadband deals, prepare transactions, monitor accounts, and switch customers to better offers

time_effort.value: some people recognize that personal agents could save time and effort

privacy_risk.value: most participants share concerns about personal data and privacy in these applications

bargaining_route.value: AI may shift consumer bargaining power, but only if authorization, verification, privacy, and commercial incentives are trustworthy

observations.method: Ofcom review of emerging agentic-AI applications and associated consumer-research findings.
observations.uncertainty: These are prospective applications, not evidence that agents currently deliver better deals or that firms will pass savings to consumers.
observations.subgroup: Telecoms customers, small businesses, AI-agent users, firms, data intermediaries, and consumers with limited time or bargaining capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Agentic tools could create new lock-in, biased recommendations, unauthorized changes, or surveillance even when they appear convenient.

observations.period: September 2026; regulatory boundary for AI customer service

transparency.value: customers should be clearly told when they are interacting with a GenAI application

gatekeeper_risk.value: Ofcom would be concerned if AI applications created barriers to support channels that providers are required to make available

harm_monitoring.value: Ofcom reports limited evidence that AI has so far been a systemic cause of harm to telecoms customers, while committing to monitor developments

accountability_route.value: consumer AI becomes a public-systems issue when automation mediates access to essential communications and complaint remedies

observations.method: Ofcom regulatory review and stated expectations for telecoms providers and AI developers.
observations.uncertainty: The regulatory position may evolve as evidence of benefit, exclusion, privacy loss, or consumer harm accumulates.
observations.subgroup: Telecoms customers, people needing complaints or complex support, providers, AI developers, and consumer-protection bodies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Strong disclosure and escalation rules may preserve accountability while allowing automation to handle routine navigation efficiently.

related_sources.claim: Ofcom's wider media and online-use research provides complementary context for AI adoption and digital behavior.
Pew data-center attitudes provide complementary public legitimacy context for AI infrastructure.

boundary: This record adds a consumer-technology route from AI use in telecoms navigation through human support, personal-agent bargaining, privacy, transparency, and regulatory access. It uses aggregate tracker and qualitative findings, not individual service histories, causal consumer outcomes, or proof that AI improves telecoms markets.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Ofcom publication was reviewed for publication date, Technology Tracker shares, qualitative human-support findings, prospective agentic-AI uses, privacy concerns, transparency expectations, gatekeeper risk, and harm-monitoring position.
